questions.prompt: With damping \(\mu > 0\), a Levenberg-Marquardt step solves
options: \(J_r^T J_r\, d = -J_r^T r\), and then discards \(d\) if \(\mu\) is positive
\(\mu\, d = J_r^T r\)
\(J_r\, d = 0\) with no use of the residual
\((J_r^T J_r + \mu I)\, d = -J_r^T r\)
questions.explanation: The damped normal equations add \(\mu I\) to the Gauss-Newton matrix and keep the same right-hand side \(-J_r^T r\). Dropping the step whenever \(\mu\) is positive would never move. The equation \(\mu d = J_r^T r\) has the wrong sign and omits \(J_r^T J_r\). A step in the null space of \(J_r\) does not reduce the linear model.

questions.prompt: A scalar parameter has \(J^T J = 2\) and \(J^T r = 4\). With damping \(\mu = 2\), what is the Levenberg-Marquardt step \(d\)?
questions.explanation: The damped equation is \((2 + 2)\, d = -4\), so \(4d = -4\) and \(d = -1\). The undamped Gauss-Newton step would be \(-4/2 = -2\), twice as long. Reporting \(1\) drops the minus sign on the right-hand side. Reporting \(-2\) forgets to add \(\mu\). Reporting \(-4\) stops at the right-hand side.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.

questions.prompt: As the damping \(\mu\) grows, with \(J^T r \ne 0\), the Levenberg-Marquardt step
options: becomes orthogonal to the gradient
stops depending on \(\mu\) once \(\mu > 1\)
shrinks like \(1/\mu\) and lines up with the negative gradient
grows without bound
questions.explanation: For large \(\mu\), \((J^T J + \mu I)^{-1}\) is about \(I/\mu\), so \(d \approx -(J^T r)/\mu\). That is a short steepest-descent step. The factor \(1/\mu\) gets smaller, so the step does not grow. The direction stays opposite the gradient rather than perpendicular to it. The formula keeps \(\mu\) in the denominator for every positive value, including values above one.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: Put an accepted damping update in order. Each step uses the result of the step before it.
questions.explanation: The trial step has to exist before its decrease can be compared with the model. Acceptance uses that comparison: the step is kept only when the true decrease is a large enough fraction of the prediction. The damping falls only after that acceptance. A rejected step is the other branch of the same test, and it raises \(\mu\) instead of lowering it. The two branches are alternatives, not successive steps.

steps: Solve \((J_r^T J_r + \mu I)\, d = -J_r^T r\) at the current damping.
Compare the true decrease in \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) with the decrease predicted by the linear model.
Accept the point plus \(d\) because that true decrease is large enough.
Decrease \(\mu\) for the next iteration after the step has been accepted.

questions.prompt: Which statements about the damping \(\mu\) hold?
options: Raising \(\mu\) shortens the step when \(J^T r \ne 0\).
As \(\mu\) tends to \(0\), the step tends to the Gauss-Newton step when \(J^T J\) is invertible.
For large \(\mu\) the direction approaches the negative gradient.
Any \(\mu > 0\) makes \(J^T J + \mu I\) singular.
\(J^T J + \mu I\) is positive definite for every \(\mu > 0\).
questions.explanation:
With \(J^T J = 2\) and \(J^T r = 4\), the step is \(-4/(2 + \mu)\). Its length is \(1\) at \(\mu = 2\) and \(0.5\) at \(\mu = 6\), so a larger damping is a shorter step.
• At \(\mu = 0\) the same formula is \(-4/2 = -2\), the Gauss-Newton step.
• The step is negative and the gradient \(4\) is positive, so the direction is the negative gradient for every \(\mu\), and the large-\(\mu\) reading is the same direction with a vanishing length.
• The scalar \(2 + \mu\) is at least \(2\) when \(\mu > 0\), so the shifted matrix is not singular. In several variables, \(v^T J^T J v + \mu\lVert v\rVert^2 \ge \mu\lVert v\rVert^2 > 0\) for \(v \ne 0\).
• A positive damping therefore cannot make the shifted matrix singular.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that falls toward the horizontal axis.

questions.prompt: A scalar parameter has residual entries \(a\) and \(b\), Jacobian entries \(p\) and \(q\), and damping \(\mu\). The damped step equals
questions.explanation: The damped Gram entry is \(p^2 + q^2 + \mu\), and the right-hand side is still \(-(pa + qb)\). Every name appears: the residual entries, the Jacobian entries, and the damping. Dropping \(\mu\) is the undamped Gauss-Newton step. Putting \(\mu\) in the numerator treats the damping as a residual. A minus sign on \(\mu\) in the denominator can make the matrix indefinite, which is not this update.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a column of two labels</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">p</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">q</text></svg>

questions.prompt: A note damps the scalar problem with \(J^T J = 2\) and \(J^T r = 4\), whose objective \(\tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) equals \(5\) at the current point. Exactly one step is a false claim.
questions.explanation: The gradient term and the Gram entry match the problem. With \(\mu = 2\) the equation \((2 + 2)d = -4\) gives \(d = -1\). For the residual \((u + 3,\ u + 1)\) at \(u = 0\), the objective is \(5\), and at \(u = -1\) it is \(2\), so the true objective did fall and the step is accepted. An accepted step is a reason to decrease the damping, not to increase it. The accepted point is the old point plus the step.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping downward on labeled axes.
steps: The undamped gradient term is \(J^T r = 4\), and \(J^T J = 2\).
With \(\mu = 2\) the damped equation gives the step \(d = -1\).
The objective falls from \(5\) to \(2\), so the step is accepted and the next damping should be larger than \(2\).
The accepted point is the current point plus \(d\).
reasons: An accepted step decreases the damping. Increasing it is the response to a rejected step.
The objective does not fall from \(5\) to \(2\).

questions.prompt: A scalar parameter has \(J^T J = 2\) and \(J^T r = 4\). With damping \(\mu = 14\), what is the step \(d\)?
questions.explanation: The equation is \((2 + 14)\, d = -4\), so \(16d = -4\) and \(d = -1/4 = -0.25\). Compared with the step \(-1\) at \(\mu = 2\), the larger damping is shorter and still negative. Reporting \(0.25\) drops the sign. Reporting \(-4/14\) forgets to add \(J^T J\). Reporting \(-2\) is the undamped step.
questions.figure_alt: A curve that drops at first and then flattens.

questions.prompt: If \(J_r\) does not have full column rank, a positive damping still produces a step because
options: a singular Gram matrix is left unchanged
\(J_r^T J_r + \mu I\) is positive definite, so it is invertible, and the step is a descent direction
the damping sets every residual to zero
the damping makes the Jacobian square
questions.explanation: For \(\mu > 0\) and \(v \ne 0\), \(v^T(J_r^T J_r + \mu I)v \ge \mu\lVert v\rVert^2 > 0\). The shifted matrix is positive definite even when \(J_r^T J_r\) is only semidefinite, so the step exists. The directional derivative equals \(-(J_r^T r)^T (J_r^T J_r + \mu I)^{-1}(J_r^T r)\), which is negative when the gradient is not zero. Damping does not zero the residual, and it does not change the shape of \(J_r\). Leaving a singular matrix unchanged is the undamped method, which is the case this shift avoids.

questions.prompt: A diagonal shift added to a Hessian, so that a Newton step for minimization becomes a descent direction, is the same idea as
options: the damping term \(\mu I\) in a Levenberg-Marquardt step
a simplex ratio test
dropping the gradient and keeping only the residual
replacing the step by an eigenvalue
questions.explanation: Both moves add a positive multiple of the identity to a matrix that may fail to be positive definite. The damped Gauss-Newton matrix and a shifted Hessian then define a descent direction. A ratio test chooses a leaving variable in the simplex method. Dropping the gradient removes the right-hand side of the step equation. An eigenvalue describes a stretch; it is not the shift itself. The damping here is \(\mu\), not an eigenvalue.

questions.prompt: With \(J^T J = 2\), \(J^T r = 4\), and \(\mu = 2\), the step is \(-1\). What is the directional derivative of \(f = \tfrac12\lVert r\rVert^2\) along that step?
questions.explanation: The gradient is \(4\) and the step is \(-1\), so the directional derivative is \(4 \cdot (-1) = -4\). The same value is \(-16 / (2 + 2)\). Reporting \(4\) drops the step. Reporting \(-1\) is the step, not the derivative. Reporting \(-2\) is the undamped Gauss-Newton step.

questions.prompt: If a damped step barely decreases the true residual beside the linear prediction, the damping update
options: accepts the step and decreases \(\mu\)
sets \(\mu\) to zero and keeps the step
replaces \(\mu\) by the residual norm and skips the comparison
rejects the step and increases \(\mu\)
questions.explanation: A small ratio of true decrease to predicted decrease says the linear model was optimistic. The trial is rejected and \(\mu\) grows, which shortens the next trial. Accepting and decreasing \(\mu\) is the response when the model agrees with the true decrease. Setting \(\mu\) to zero returns to plain Gauss-Newton on a step the model just failed to justify. The residual norm can be part of the comparison, but it does not replace the increase in damping.
questions.figure_alt: A straight line sloping upward on labeled axes.
